titre: Indirect questions (Could you tell me where…?)
intro: Indirect questions (“Could you tell me where the station is?”) are more polite than direct questions (“Where is the station?”). They are essential with strangers, at work, at a hotel reception or on the phone. The trap: the word order goes back to that of a normal statement.
objectifs: Turn a direct question into a polite indirect question with the main opening phrases.
Use subject + verb order and remove do / does / did.
Use if / whether for yes / no questions.
Choose the right punctuation and avoid the most common mistakes.

texte: A direct question can sound abrupt when you speak to a stranger or a customer. Starting with a phrase like “Could you tell me…”, “Do you know…” or “I was wondering…” makes it softer and more polite.
Indirect questions also express doubt or personal thoughts: “I wonder why she left.”
In the indirect part, the subject and verb are not inverted: we go back to subject + verb order, as in a statement. The question word (where, when, why, how much…) stays at the start of that part.
With be and modal verbs (can, will, should…), just put the subject before the verb. This is the most common mistake: “Could you tell me where is the station?” is wrong.

lignes: Could you tell me where the station is?
What time does the shop open?
Do you know what time the shop opens?
Can you tell me how much it cost?
When will the results be ready?
Do you know when the results will be ready?
Could you explain why we can't park here?

texte: In a direct question in the present simple or past simple, we use do / does / did. In the indirect question these helpers disappear, and the verb goes back to its normal form: -s for he / she / it, or the past form.
A tip: imagine the statement (“The shop opens at nine”) and put it after the question word.
exemples: Where does she work? → Do you know where she works?
What did he say? → Can you tell me what he said?
How do I get to the airport? → Could you tell me how I get to the airport?
Also possible: how to get to the airport.

sections.titre: Yes / no questions: if or whether
texte: When the direct question expects a yes / no answer (Is…? Do…? Can…?), there is no question word: use “if” or “whether”. “Whether” is a little more formal and often goes with “or not”.
This “if” is not the “if” of conditions: it introduces a yes / no question.
exemples: Is the museum open on Monday? → Do you know if the museum is open on Monday?
Can I pay by card? → Could you tell me whether I can pay by card?
Did they receive my email? → I'd like to know if they received my email.

texte: Subject questions (who, what, which + verb): the order does not change, because the question word is already the subject. “Who called? → Do you know who called?”.

“I was wondering if you could…” makes a very polite request, especially in writing: “I was wondering if you could send me the brochure.” After a past opening verb (I was wondering, I asked), you can keep the present when the situation is still true.
Indirect questions look like reported questions (lesson 105), but here you are really asking: there is no change of tense after “Do you know…” or “Could you tell me…”.
exemples: Who won the match? → Do you know who won the match?
I was wondering if you could help me with this form.

formule: Could you tell me / Do you know + question word (or if / whether) + subject + verb …?
prononciation: In “Could you tell me”, “could you” often sounds like /ˈkʊdʒuː/ and “tell me” is linked: /ˈtel mi/.
In “Do you know”, “do you” is often reduced to /djə/: /djə ˈnəʊ/ in fast speech.
An indirect question that starts with Do you know / Could you tell me usually has a rising tone at the end, like a yes / no question.
With “I wonder…” or “I'd like to know…”, the tone falls: they are statements.
erreurs: Could you tell me where is the bank?
Could you tell me where the bank is?
Subject + verb order in the indirect part.
Do you know what time does the train leave?
Do you know what time the train leaves?
Remove does and add -s.
Can you tell me what did she say?
Can you tell me what she said?
Remove did and use the past form.
Do you know is the pharmacy open?
Do you know if the pharmacy is open?
Yes / no question: if / whether.
I wonder why is he late?
I wonder why he is late.
Statement order and a full stop (it's not a question).
Could you tell me where can I park?
Could you tell me where I can park?
With a modal: subject before the modal.
I'd like to know if is it possible.
I'd like to know if it is possible.
After if: subject + verb.

dialogue.contexte: Mariam has just arrived in Toronto for an internship. She phones the student residence where she will stay.
lignes: Good morning, Maple Residence. How can I help you?
Hello. I'm arriving tomorrow and I was wondering if I could check in after 10 p.m.
Very polite request: I was wondering if…
Yes, that's fine. The night porter is here until 2 a.m.
Great. Could you tell me how I get there from the airport?
Take the UP Express to Union Station, then the subway to Spadina.
Thank you. Do you know how much the train costs?
I'm not sure exactly how much it is now, but you can check on their website.
OK. And one last thing: do you know whether the rooms have Wi-Fi?
Yes, they all do. The password is on your key card.

exercices.consigne: Is the indirect question correct (C) or incorrect (I)?
items: Do you know where the toilets are?
C
Could you tell me what time does it start?
I (what time it starts)
I wonder if she's coming.
C
Can you tell me where can I buy a ticket?
I (where I can buy)

exercices.consigne: Make the direct question indirect with the phrase given.
items: Where is the post office? (Could you tell me…)
Could you tell me where the post office is?
What time does the bank close? (Do you know…)
Do you know what time the bank closes?
How much did the tickets cost? (Can you tell me…)
Can you tell me how much the tickets cost?
Why is the flight delayed? (I'd like to know…)
I'd like to know why the flight is delayed.
When will the doctor arrive? (Do you have any idea…)
Do you have any idea when the doctor will arrive?
Who is the manager? (Do you know…)
Do you know who the manager is?
Is breakfast included? (Do you know…)
Do you know if breakfast is included?
Can I change my seat? (Could you tell me…)
Could you tell me whether I can change my seat?
Did the parcel arrive? (I was wondering…)
I was wondering if the parcel arrived / had arrived.
Does this bus go to the city centre? (Do you know…)
Do you know if this bus goes to the city centre?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: Do you know where does Paul live?
Do you know where Paul lives?
I wonder what is he doing.
I wonder what he is doing.
Could you tell me is there a pharmacy near here?
Could you tell me if there is a pharmacy near here?
Can you tell me what did the doctor say?
Can you tell me what the doctor said?

exercices.consigne: Make these direct questions more polite with an indirect question.
items: Where's the station?
Could you tell me where the station is?
Is the shop open on Sunday?
Do you know if the shop is open on Sunday?
Why didn't he answer? (thinking aloud: I wonder…)
I wonder why he didn't answer.

exercices.consigne: You are planning a trip to Brussels. Write a short email (4–5 sentences) to a hotel with at least four different indirect questions.
items: Model answer

Dear Sir or Madam, I have a reservation from 3 to 6 May. I was wondering if I could check in early, around 10 a.m. Could you tell me how I can get to the hotel from Brussels-Midi station? I'd also like to know whether breakfast is included in the price. Finally, do you know if there is a pharmacy near the hotel? Kind regards, Claire Mballa

a_retenir: Indirect question = polite phrase + question word + subject + verb (Could you tell me where the station is?).
No do / does / did: Do you know what time the shop opens?
Yes / no questions: if or whether (Do you know if it's open?).
Question mark only if the opening phrase is a question (Do you know…?); full stop after I wonder / I'd like to know.
Subject questions (who called?): the order doesn't change.
